plan.topic_summary: AI agents—systems that autonomously plan, reason, and use tools to accomplish multi-step goals—are a rapidly evolving paradigm in AI software. For a 1-5 year investment view, the key question is whether agents will transition from experimental frameworks to a dominant software architecture, and what technical, economic, and regulatory barriers must be cleared.
key_questions: What is the current state of agent reliability in production, and what are the primary failure modes that limit deployment at scale?
How are companies currently monetizing agent capabilities, and which revenue models (per-task, subscription, outcome-based) are gaining traction?
Will agent architectures converge on a dominant paradigm or remain fragmented across competing frameworks and protocols?
How do inference cost trends and model efficiency improvements affect the unit economics of agent-based products over the next 1-3 years?
What safety, alignment, and regulatory frameworks are likely to emerge for autonomous agents, and how might they constrain or shape deployment?
Will open-weight models close the capability gap with closed models for agent tasks, and what does that imply for the competitive landscape and pricing power of closed-model providers?

sources.title: AI Agents That Matter
sources.abstract: AI agents are an exciting new research direction, and agent development is driven by benchmarks. Our analysis of current agent benchmarks and evaluation practices reveals several shortcomings that hinder their usefulness in real-world applications. First, there is a narrow focus on accuracy without attention to other metrics. As a result, SOTA agents are needlessly complex and costly, and the community has reached mistaken conclusions about the sources of accuracy gains. Our focus on cost in addition to accuracy motivates the new goal of jointly optimizing the two metrics. We design and implement one such optimization, showing its potential to greatly reduce cost while maintaining accuracy. Second, the benchmarking needs of model and downstream developers have been conflated, making it hard to identify which agent would be best suited for a particular application. Third, many agent benchmarks have inadequate holdout sets, and sometimes none at all. This has led to agents that are fragile because they take shortcuts and overfit to the benchmark in various ways. We prescribe a principled framework for avoiding overfitting. Finally, there is a lack of standardization in evaluation practices, leading to a pervasive lack of reproducibility. We hope that the steps we introduce for addressing these shortcomings will spur the development of agents that are useful in the real world and not just accurate on benchmarks.

sources.title: A cybersecurity AI agent selection and decision support framework
sources.abstract: This paper presents a novel, structured decision support framework that systematically aligns diverse artificial intelligence (AI) agent architectures, reactive, cognitive, hybrid, and learning, with the comprehensive National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0. By integrating agent theory with industry guidelines, this framework provides a transparent and stepwise methodology for selecting and deploying AI solutions to address contemporary cyber threats. Employing a granular decomposition of NIST CSF 2.0 functions into specific tasks, the study links essential AI agent properties such as autonomy, adaptive learning, and real-time responsiveness to each subcategory's security requirements. In addition, it outlines graduated levels of autonomy (assisted, augmented, and fully autonomous) to accommodate organisations at varying stages of cybersecurity maturity. This holistic approach transcends isolated AI applications, providing a unified detection, incident response, and governance strategy. Through conceptual validation, the framework demonstrates how tailored AI agent deployments can align with real-world constraints and risk profiles, enhancing situational awareness, accelerating response times, and fortifying long-term resilience via adaptive risk management. Ultimately, this research bridges the gap between theoretical AI constructs and operational cybersecurity demands, establishing a foundation for robust, empirically validated multi-agent systems that adhere to industry standards.

sources.title: Visibility into AI Agents
sources.venue: ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT)
sources.abstract: Increased delegation of commercial, scientific, governmental, and personal activities to AI agents—systems capable of pursuing complex goals with limited supervision—may exacerbate existing societal risks and introduce new risks. Understanding and mitigating these risks involves critically evaluating existing governance structures, revising and adapting these structures where needed, and ensuring accountability of key stakeholders. Information about where, why, how, and by whom certain AI agents are used, which we refer to as visibility, is critical to these objectives. In this paper, we assess three categories of measures to increase visibility into AI agents: agent identifiers, real-time monitoring, and activity logging. For each, we outline potential implementations that vary in intrusiveness and informativeness. We analyze how the measures apply across a spectrum of centralized through decentralized deployment contexts, accounting for various actors in the supply chain including hardware and software service providers. Finally, we discuss the implications of our measures for privacy and concentration of power. Further work into understanding the measures and mitigating their negative impacts can help to build a foundation for the governance of AI agents.

sources.title: Safe, Untrusted, "Proof-Carrying" AI Agents: toward the agentic lakehouse
sources.abstract: Data lakehouses run sensitive workloads, where AI-driven automation raises concerns about trust, correctness, and governance. We argue that API-first, programmable lakehouses provide the right abstractions for safe-by-design, agentic workflows. Using Bauplan as a case study, we show how data branching and declarative environments extend naturally to agents, enabling reproducibility and observability while reducing the attack surface. We present a proof-of-concept in which agents repair data pipelines using correctness checks inspired by proof-carrying code. Our prototype demonstrates that untrusted AI agents can operate safely on production data and outlines a path toward a fully agentic lakehouse.

sources.title: AI Agents vs. Agentic AI: A Conceptual taxonomy, applications and challenges
sources.abstract: Information fusion, in the context of the Generative AI era, must distinguish AI Agents from Agentic AI. This review critically distinguishes between AI Agents and Agentic AI, offering a structured, conceptual taxonomy, application mapping, and analysis of opportunities and challenges to clarify their divergent design philosophies and capabilities. We begin by outlining the search strategy and foundational definitions, characterizing AI Agents as modular systems driven and enabled by LLMs and LIMs for task-specific automation. Generative AI is positioned as a precursor providing the foundation, with AI agents advancing through tool integration, prompt engineering, and reasoning enhancements. We then characterize Agentic AI systems, which, in contrast to AI Agents, represent a paradigm shift marked by multi-agent collaboration, dynamic task decomposition, persistent memory, and coordinated autonomy. Through a chronological evaluation of architectural evolution, operational mechanisms, interaction styles, and autonomy levels, we present a comparative analysis across both AI agents and agentic AI paradigms. Application domains enabled by AI Agents such as customer support, scheduling, and data summarization are then contrasted with Agentic AI deployments in research automation, robotic coordination, and medical decision support. We further examine unique challenges in each paradigm including hallucination, brittleness, emergent behavior, and coordination failure, and propose targeted solutions such as ReAct loops, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), automation coordination layers, and causal modeling. This work aims to provide a roadmap for developing robust, scalable, and explainable AI-driven systems.

sources.title: What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation
sources.abstract: Bot detectors deployed at scale treat traffic as binary: human or bot. This assumption breaks when AI agents browse the web through browser automation, a traffic class that is neither and that binary classifiers structurally cannot represent. We present a three-class detection framework distinguishing humans, bots, and AI agents, and show that the binary-vs-agent confusion is architectural: a binary human-vs-bot detector misroutes agent sessions because its label space lacks an agent class. On our controlled benchmark, an MLP binary classifier misclassifies 39.1% of real AI agents as human and a SAINT binary transformer misclassifies 34.5%; adding an explicit agent class yields per-class agent F1 = 1.000 in all 30 runs (3 model families $\times$ 10 seeds). To measure evasion resistance, we construct a five-level evasion ladder spanning passive observation, GAN-generated trajectories, and replay of real human cursor data ($n = 2299$ evasion sessions). Across 10 seeds and 3 model families we observe zero agent misses in 22990 per-seed predictions. The discriminative signal is a browser-automation artifact, not evidence of agent reasoning: Playwright does not emit the raw pointer-move and wheel-delta streams a physical input device produces, and this absence signature survives trajectory manipulation. Exhaustive search over all feature subsets of size 1-5 (9401 GBMs) shows that two behavioral features (mouse_event_rate, teleport_click_ratio) give 100% observed agent recall at every evasion level with agent precision 0.994; five features lift macro-F1 to 0.991. The signal is redundantly encoded: removing teleport_click_ratio leaves agent detection at 100%. The single-feature regime is degenerate, flagging every agent only by collapsing the classifier to always predict "agent". Two features robustly isolate agents; five separate all three traffic classes at macro-F1 $\geq 0.99$.

sources.title: Governing AI Agents
Continuous Process-Level Evaluation for Evolving Enterprise AI Agent Skills
sources.abstract: Enterprise AI agent skills evolve as tool APIs, models, and specifications change, yet final-output evaluation can miss process-level behavioral drift. We present a continuous evaluation framework combining outcome-level and process-level checks, applied to Revenue and Productivity variants of a Business Value Determination skill in an enterprise Value Aware Resiliency system. The framework independently computes per-run ground truth, materializes reusable template tests, and evaluates tool selection, arguments, execution order, and database integrity through programmatic checks and a narrowly scoped LLM judge. We evaluate 240 trials across two skills, two specification variants, two agent harnesses, and three models. Of 175 trials passing all applicable final numerical checks, 162 (92.6 percent; Wilson 95 percent CI: 87.7-95.6 percent) contained another evaluator-detected deviation. Under a broader seven-check final-state definition, 151 of 164 passing runs (92.1 percent; 95 percent CI: 86.9-95.3 percent) still violated a trajectory check. Dependency attribution reduced a mean of 6.34 failed checks per run to 2.65 roots. Specification sensitivity varied by model and harness, with exploratory bootstrap interaction intervals excluding zero for all three Revenue comparisons and one of three Productivity comparisons. Runtime-resolved templates provided reusable regression coverage across the evaluated configurations; longitudinal validation under actual API evolution remains future work.

sources.title: Empowering biomedical discovery with AI agents
sources.abstract: We envision "AI scientists" as systems capable of skeptical learning and reasoning that empower biomedical research through collaborative agents that integrate AI models and biomedical tools with experimental platforms. Rather than taking humans out of the discovery process, biomedical AI agents combine human creativity and expertise with AI's ability to analyze large datasets, navigate hypothesis spaces, and execute repetitive tasks. AI agents are poised to be proficient in various tasks, planning discovery workflows and performing self-assessment to identify and mitigate gaps in their knowledge. These agents use large language models and generative models to feature structured memory for continual learning and use machine learning tools to incorporate scientific knowledge, biological principles, and theories. AI agents can impact areas ranging from virtual cell simulation, programmable control of phenotypes, and the design of cellular circuits to developing new therapies.

sources.title: Foundations of a Time-Consistent Counterfactual Actuarial Runtime for Autonomous AI Agents
sources.abstract: We propose a foundational runtime actuarial layer for autonomous AI agents in which every side-effect-bearing action carries a time-consistent, counterfactual risk toll computed against a contractually fixed safe default, inside an explicit underwriting boundary. The framework treats per-action insurance as the primary unit of analysis and replaces post-hoc annual liability cover with a pre-action transaction layer. The paper establishes four structural results: (i) a well-defined counterfactual toll under a chosen safe-default mapping and continuation policy, with explicit non-uniqueness; (ii) a no-splitting property within an underwriting boundary that telescopes path-decomposed actions into a boundary potential, with a corollary tying gaming-resistance to boundary design; (iii) an irreversible-authority premium, split into a strictly positive action-level component and an if-and-only-if characterisation of the set-level robust capital increase; and (iv) a conservative runtime gating theorem that translates high-probability toll envelopes into an executed-action budget guarantee. The result is the mathematical base layer for a broader program: an empirical companion instantiates the runtime through an Actuarial Action Interface and authority-frontier experiments; a mechanism-design companion studies strategic operator incentives and cross-boundary aggregation; and a dynamic-underwriting companion studies experience rating and audit-replay calibration. The present paper states the primitive contract, the toll identity, the within-boundary no-arbitrage result, and the budget guarantee on which those later layers depend.

sources.title: Cryptographically verifiable authorization for autonomous AI agents: a falsifiable hypothesis and proof of concept
sources.abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly execute actions, invoke tools, and operate on protected resources with limited human oversight. Existing authentication and authorization mechanisms establish identity and delegate authority but do not inherently provide cryptographic evidence that a concrete request issued by a specific agent satisfies the applicable policy in a specific execution context. This study hypothesizes that agent authorization can be formalized as a cryptographically verifiable relation, denoted $R_{CVA}$, that jointly binds an agent principal, a concrete authorization request, an execution context, and the satisfaction of an applicable policy, while selectively preserving the confidentiality of private authorization attributes. We introduce a preliminary formal abstraction for Cryptographically Verifiable Agent Authorization (CVA), define a compact set of candidate security properties including authorization soundness, principal binding, request binding, policy binding, and replay resistance, and provide an executable zero-knowledge proof of concept that instantiates selected elements of the model over a Groth16 zk-SNARK construction. We further identify and formalize the structural separation among identity binding, authorization-request binding, and runtime execution binding as a central open problem in the design of secure agentic systems, a distinction to our knowledge, has not been formalized within a cryptographically verifiable authorization relation by current agentic security frameworks, and present a falsifiable research agenda for its resolution.

sources.title: Infrastructure for AI Agents
sources.abstract: AI agents plan and execute interactions in open-ended environments. For example, OpenAI's Operator can use a web browser to do product comparisons and buy online goods. Much research on making agents useful and safe focuses on directly modifying their behaviour, such as by training them to follow user instructions. Direct behavioural modifications are useful, but do not fully address how heterogeneous agents will interact with each other and other actors. Rather, we will need external protocols and systems to shape such interactions. For instance, agents will need more efficient protocols to communicate with each other and form agreements. Attributing an agent's actions to a particular human or other legal entity can help to establish trust, and also disincentivize misuse. Given this motivation, we propose the concept of \textbf{agent infrastructure}: technical systems and shared protocols external to agents that are designed to mediate and influence their interactions with and impacts on their environments. Just as the Internet relies on protocols like HTTPS, our work argues that agent infrastructure will be similarly indispensable to ecosystems of agents. We identify three functions for agent infrastructure: 1) attributing actions, properties, and other information to specific agents, their users, or other actors; 2) shaping agents' interactions; and 3) detecting and remedying harmful actions from agents. We provide an incomplete catalog of research directions for such functions. For each direction, we include analysis of use cases, infrastructure adoption, relationships to existing (internet) infrastructure, limitations, and open questions. Making progress on agent infrastructure can prepare society for the adoption of more advanced agents.

sources.title: Security of AI Agents
sources.abstract: AI agents have been boosted by large language models. AI agents can function as intelligent assistants and complete tasks on behalf of their users with access to tools and the ability to execute commands in their environments. Through studying and experiencing the workflow of typical AI agents, we have raised several concerns regarding their security. These potential vulnerabilities are not addressed by the frameworks used to build the agents, nor by research aimed at improving the agents. In this paper, we identify and describe these vulnerabilities in detail from a system security perspective, emphasizing their causes and severe effects. Furthermore, we introduce defense mechanisms corresponding to each vulnerability with design and experiments to evaluate their viability. Altogether, this paper contextualizes the security issues in the current development of AI agents and delineates methods to make AI agents safer and more reliable.

sources.title: AI Agents and Agentic Systems: A Multi-Expert Analysis
sources.abstract: The emergence of AI agents and agentic systems represents a significant milestone in artificial intelligence, enabling autonomous systems to operate, learn, and collaborate in complex environments with minimal human intervention. This paper, drawing on multi-expert perspectives, examines the potential of AI agents and agentic systems to reshape industries by decentralizing decision-making, redefining organizational structures, and enhancing cross-functional collaboration. Specific applications include healthcare systems capable of creating adaptive treatment plans, supply chain agents that predict and address disruptions in real-time, and business process automation that reallocates tasks from humans to AI, improving efficiency and innovation. However, the integration of these systems raises critical challenges, including issues of attribution and shared accountability in decision-making, compatibility with legacy systems, and addressing biases in AI-driven processes. The paper concludes that while agentic systems hold immense promise, robust governance frameworks, cross-industry collaboration, and interdisciplinary research into ethical design are essential. Future research should explore adaptive workforce reskilling strategies, transparent accountability mechanisms, and energy-efficient deployment models to ensure ethical and scalable implementation.

sources.title: Preregistration for Experiments with AI Agents
sources.abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and autonomous AI agents has given rise to a rapidly growing methodological paradigm: "in silico" behavioral experiments. Originally conceived as a way to use AI agents as proxies for human participants in studies of cognition, decision-making, and social dynamics, this approach has taken on new significance -- as AI agents increasingly negotiate, transact, and make consequential decisions on behalf of people and organizations, understanding their behavior has become a research priority in its own right. While these experiments with AI agents offer unprecedented advantages in terms of scalability, cost efficiency, and experimental control, they also inherit, and in some cases amplify, methodological vulnerabilities that have long plagued human subjects research. To address these issues, this paper argues that preregistration practices -- central to improving the credibility of human subjects experiments -- should now be extended to experiments with AI agents. We systematically catalog the researcher degrees of freedom that experiments with AI agents introduce -- model selection, prompt wording, settings, and outcome-contingent redesign, for example -- and show how the low cost of iteration and lack of reporting norms make these choices both easy to exploit and difficult to detect. We propose a preregistration template tailored to experiments with AI agents and call on conferences, journals, and funding agencies to make preregistration standard practice for this emerging research paradigm.

sources.title: Authenticated Delegation and Authorized AI Agents
sources.abstract: The rapid deployment of autonomous AI agents creates urgent challenges around authorization, accountability, and access control in digital spaces. New standards are needed to know whom AI agents act on behalf of and guide their use appropriately, protecting online spaces while unlocking the value of task delegation to autonomous agents. We introduce a novel framework for authenticated, authorized, and auditable delegation of authority to AI agents, where human users can securely delegate and restrict the permissions and scope of agents while maintaining clear chains of accountability. This framework builds on existing identification and access management protocols, extending OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect with agent-specific credentials and metadata, maintaining compatibility with established authentication and web infrastructure. Further, we propose a framework for translating flexible, natural language permissions into auditable access control configurations, enabling robust scoping of AI agent capabilities across diverse interaction modalities. Taken together, this practical approach facilitates immediate deployment of AI agents while addressing key security and accountability concerns, working toward ensuring agentic AI systems perform only appropriate actions and providing a tool for digital service providers to enable AI agent interactions without risking harm from scalable interaction.

sources.title: A Hierarchical Failure Taxonomy for Reliability Assessment of AI Agents: An Empirical Analysis of the Agent Failure Atlas 2026 Benchmark
sources.abstract: As large language model (LLM) based applications evolve into autonomous, action oriented AI agents, their evaluation can no longer rely on binary success/failure metrics.Agentic systems operate through dynamic, multi-step interactions with tools and environments, introducing complex failure modes that propagate and cascade.This study presents a hierarchical failure taxonomy and an empirical reliability assessment using the Agent Failure Atlas 2026 benchmark.Analyzing 3,336 agent runs encompassing 43,477 trajectory steps and 3,802 failure events, we characterize agent reliability across four dimensions: frequency, criticality, cascading behavior, and recoverability.Our results reveal a two dimensional reliability landscape: high prevalence but largely recoverable failures (e.g., tool use and state tracking errors) contrast sharply with low prevalence but highly critical failures (e.g., validation and output errors).Furthermore, we show that intermediate failures often resolve through agent self correction, decoupling run level error rates from final task success.By shifting the analytical focus from isolated outcome accuracy to mechanistic failure propagation, this framework provides a foundational methodology for reliability engineering, risk mitigation, and the safe deployment of autonomous AI systems.

sources.title: IBGP: Imperfect Byzantine Generals Problem for Zero-Shot Robustness in Communicative Multi-Agent Systems
sources.abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents increasingly integrate into our infrastructure, their robust coordination and message synchronization become vital. The Byzantine Generals Problem (BGP) is a critical model for constructing resilient multi-agent systems (MAS) under adversarial attacks. It describes a scenario where malicious agents with unknown identities exist in the system-situations that, in our context, could result from LLM agents' hallucinations or external attacks. In BGP, the objective of the entire system is to reach a consensus on the action to be taken. Traditional BGP requires global consensus among all agents; however, in practical scenarios, global consensus is not always necessary and can even be inefficient. Therefore, there is a pressing need to explore a refined version of BGP that aligns with the local coordination patterns observed in MAS. We refer to this refined version as Imperfect BGP (IBGP) in our research, aiming to address this discrepancy. To tackle this issue, we propose a framework that leverages consensus protocols within general MAS settings, providing provable resilience against communication attacks and adaptability to changing environments, as validated by empirical results. Additionally, we present a case study in a sensor network environment to illustrate the practical application of our protocol.

sources.title: From Failure Modes to Reliability Awareness in Generative and Agentic AI System
Agent Safety Alignment via Reinforcement Learning
sources.abstract: The emergence of autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents capable of tool usage has introduced new safety risks that go beyond traditional conversational misuse. These agents, empowered to execute external functions, are vulnerable to both user-initiated threats (e.g., adversarial prompts) and tool-initiated threats (e.g., malicious outputs from compromised tools). In this paper, we propose the first unified safety-alignment framework for tool-using agents, enabling models to handle both channels of threat via structured reasoning and sandboxed reinforcement learning. We introduce a tri-modal taxonomy, including benign, malicious, and sensitive for both user prompts and tool responses, and define a policy-driven decision model. Our framework employs a custom-designed sandbox environment that simulates real-world tool execution and allows fine-grained reward shaping. Through extensive evaluations on public and self-built benchmarks, including Agent SafetyBench, InjecAgent, and BFCL, we demonstrate that our safety-aligned agents significantly improve resistance to security threats while preserving strong utility on benign tasks. Our results show that safety and effectiveness can be jointly optimized, laying the groundwork for trustworthy deployment of autonomous LLM agents.

sources.title: Evaluating Reliability of LLM-Based Agentic AI Systems: A Failure Taxonomy and the Agent Reliability Assurance Framework
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents can plan, call tools, browse the web, write code and act in digital environments with limited human supervision. As these systems move from generating text to changing external state, reliability becomes broader than single-response accuracy. This paper presents a structured narrative review and conceptual synthesis of reliability evaluation for LLMbased agents. It organises representative benchmarks by environment, task horizon, interaction type and reliability signal; synthesises recurring failures into six families—planning and reasoning, grounding and perception, tool use, memory and context, multi-agent coordination, and safety and security; and proposes the Agent Reliability Assurance Framework (ARAF). ARAF connects five assurance layers—capability and permission, reasoning and control, runtime monitoring, evaluation and benchmarking, and governance and accountability—to prevention, detection, verification and deployment decisions. The paper further proposes a six-metric reporting profile covering single-trial success, repeated-trial consistency, robustness, safety violations, recovery and cost. No new experimental results are claimed. Instead, the paper specifies a validation plan and argues that reliability should be reported as a multidimensional profile rather than a single benchmark score. The framework provides a common vocabulary for diagnosing failures and for determining when an agent is ready for greater operational autonomy.

sources.title: TAME: A Trustworthy Test-Time Evolution of Agent Memory with Systematic Benchmarking
sources.abstract: Test-time evolution of agent memory represents a pivotal paradigm for advancing AGI, as it strengthens complex reasoning through experience accumulation without requiring parameter updates. However, even during benign task evolution, agent safety alignment remains vulnerable, a phenomenon known as Agent Memory Misevolution. To evaluate this phenomenon, we construct the Trust-Memevo benchmark and find that agents exhibit an overall decline in trustworthiness across multiple tasks during benign task evolution. To address this issue, we propose TAME, a trust-aware memory evolution framework in which a shared memory bank is jointly governed by an Executor and an Evaluator. The Executor retrieves and applies transferable experiences to support task solving, while the Evaluator assesses the contribution of each utilized experience to the outcome and produces trust-aware feedback to guide subsequent memory use. This executor-evaluator loop enables memory to be selectively reinforced, cautiously reused, and continuously expanded over time. Experiments show that TAME mitigates memory misevolution while achieving strong task performance. In particular, on the GPT-5.2 AIME benchmark, TAME improves accuracy by 14.6 percentage points over the strongest existing method and maintains competitive trustworthiness.

sources.title: SafeEvolve: Harness-Policy Co-Evolution from Agent Experience for Safety Alignment
sources.abstract: The performance of LLM-based agents is jointly shaped by the base model and the harness used when interacting with the environment. This exposes them to safety risks in both harmful final responses and multi-step execution trajectories. Existing safety alignment mechanisms often rely on either external harness updates or policy optimization, yet applying either paradigm in isolation fails to bridge runtime control with intrinsic safety. We propose SafeEvolve, an experience-driven self-evolving framework for agent safety alignment. SafeEvolve leverages safety experience from completed on-policy trajectories to drive a continual loop of harness-policy co-evolution. On the harness side, SafeEvolve converts trajectory-level safety evidence into bounded, component-level updates across safety prompt and hierarchical skills, yielding auditable and reversible harness artifacts. On the policy side, SafeEvolve follows a two-stage SFT-RL paradigm, where harness-use SFT bootstraps the policy to actively leverage evolved harness artifacts, and harness-augmented RL further shapes autonomous safety behaviors during multi-step exploration via verifier-decomposed rewards. Through harness-policy co-evolution, SafeEvolve converts safety experience into an evolved runtime harness and improved policy behavior. Experiments on agentic safety benchmarks show that SafeEvolve achieves a stronger safety-utility tradeoff than existing baselines. For Qwen3.5-4B, SafeEvolve achieves a $3\times$ ASR reduction on AgentDojo while improving benign utility from 59.79% to 61.86%.

sources.title: On-Policy Self-Evolution via Failure Trajectories for Agentic Safety Alignment
sources.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents fail through trajectories rather than only final responses, as they may execute unsafe tool calls, follow injected instructions, comply with harmful requests, or over-refuse benign tasks despite producing a seemingly safe answer. Existing safety-alignment signals are largely response-level or off-policy, and often incur a safety-utility trade-off: improving agent safety comes at the cost of degraded task performance. Such sparse and single-objective rewards severely limit real-world usability. To bridge this gap, we propose FATE, an on-policy self-evolving framework that transforms verifier-scored failures into repair supervision without expert demonstrations. For each failure, the same policy proposes repair candidates, which are then re-scored by verifiers and filtered across security, utility, over-refusal control, and trajectory validity. This dense trajectory-level information is then used as a supervision signal for agent self-evolution. During this process, we further introduce Pareto-Front Policy Optimization (PFPO), combining supervised warmup with Pareto-aware policy optimization to preserve safety-utility trade-offs. Experiments on AgentDojo, AgentHarm, and ATBench show that FATE improves safety across different models and scales while preserving useful behavior. Compared with strong baselines, FATE reduces attack success rate by 33.5%, harmful compliance by 82.6%, and improves external trajectory-safety diagnosis by 6.5%. These results suggest that failed trajectories can provide structured repair supervision for safer self-evolving agents.

sources.title: AgentDoG 1.5: A Lightweight and Scalable Alignment Framework for AI Agent Safety and Security
sources.abstract: Modern open-world agents such as OpenClaw exhibit powerful cross-environment execution capabilities yet introduce broad new safety risk sources. Meanwhile, advanced frontier AI models drastically lower attack barriers, rendering current agent alignment frameworks inadequate for real-world deployment. To tackle these emerging threats, we propose a lightweight and scalable agent safety alignment framework. Specifically, we update the agent safety taxonomy to accommodate emergent risks from Codex and OpenClaw execution scenarios. We further build a taxonomy-guided data engine with influence-function purification to train lightweight AgentDoG 1.5 variants (0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 8B parameters) using only around 1k samples, achieving comparable performance with leading closed-source models (e.g., GPT-5.4). Based on AgentDoG 1.5, we construct a highly efficient agentic safety SFT and RL training environment, which reduces deployment overhead in Docker-level environments by two orders of magnitude. Finally, we deploy AgentDoG 1.5 as a training-free online guardrail for real-time safety moderation. Extensive experimental results indicate that AgentDoG 1.5 achieves state-of-the-art performance in diverse and complex interactive agentic scenarios. All models and datasets are openly released.

sources.title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution
sources.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to solve real-world problems, and their effectiveness depends on both the underlying models and the harnesses that support their operation. However, most existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities and overall agent performance, with limited attention to the evaluation of agent harnesses. To address this gap, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components covering context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. We construct 95 expert-level, mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth to support semantically equivalent comparisons while preserving the native behavior of each harness. We design a Trajectory Tracing (TT) module to capture agent execution traces and introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separately assesses agent performance and harness reliability. In addition, we design a Multi-source Evidence Acquisition (MEA) module to provide evidence from the agent context, harness, and execution environment for LLM-based evaluation, and develop a Failure Attribution (FA) module that uses explicit mechanism chains to support attribution at the run level. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 95 tasks, our evaluation of 3,420 runs yields macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. TraceTrial-Bench provides an auditable and reproducible foundation for comparing agent harnesses, diagnosing their failures, and studying how harness design interacts with model behavior.

sources.title: Trajectory Reliability Prediction for Generalist AI Agents: Tool-Use Failure Analysis and Success Forecasting on ZClawBench
sources.venue: Journal of Technology Informatics and Engineering
sources.abstract: Generalist AI agents increasingly perform complex tasks through planning, tool execution, action revision, and artifact generation rather than isolated response generation. This study empirically investigates trajectory reliability prediction on ZClawBench, a public OpenClaw-style agent benchmark containing 696 model-task trajectories across 116 tasks, six model families, and six scenario categories. The study evaluates whether operational trajectory signals—including tool-call volume, replanning behavior, tool errors, invalid-action ratio, recovery patterns, looping indicators, trajectory length, and task category—can predict task success before manual evaluation. Since the dataset provides trajectories and identifiers but lacks explicit per-instance success labels, the binary target is reconstructed from official model-by-category score distributions and treated as a modeling assumption. Five-fold cross-validation with task-level splitting was applied to prevent task leakage. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, sequence TF-IDF classification, and a rubric-based trajectory judge were compared. Logistic Regression achieved the strongest calibrated performance, obtaining ROC-AUC of 0.970, F1-score of 0.913, Brier score of 0.066, and expected calibration error of 0.018. Feature analysis indicated that task difficulty, no-progress behavior, response size, tool errors, and invalid actions contributed most to reliability prediction. The findings suggest that lightweight trajectory diagnostics can support agent monitoring, failure triage, and routing decisions, while further validation with direct case-level evaluation labels is required for deployment claims.

findings.claim: Agent failures differ sharply in severity. Frequent failures such as tool-use and state-tracking errors are largely recoverable, while rarer failures such as validation and output errors are highly critical. Failures can also cascade across steps, so average error rates understate tail risk.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This rests on a single abstract from a small journal with 0 citations. The 'Agent Failure Atlas 2026' benchmark cannot be checked here. The 3,336 runs are a moderate sample, and the abstract does not say how many tasks, models or domains they cover.
findings.supporting_excerpt: high prevalence but largely recoverable failures (e.g., tool use and state tracking errors) contrast sharply with low prevalence but highly critical failures (e.g., validation and output errors)

findings.claim: Final task success can hide unreliable agent behaviour. In one benchmark, about 31% of successful runs still failed at least one harness reliability criterion, and harness scores varied widely across harnesses. A separate study found run-level error rates decoupled from final success.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The TraceTrial-Bench result is an arXiv preprint, so it is not peer reviewed. Its evaluation uses LLM-based evidence modules, and the 95 tasks are authored by the benchmark's creators. Read together, the two papers suggest that outcome-only scores can overstate production readiness. Self-correction can also mask underlying errors. That synthesis is my interpretation.
findings.supporting_excerpt: 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion

findings.claim: Agents that learn from accumulated memory can become less trustworthy over time, even on benign tasks. A decline in trustworthiness with continual 'self-evolution' is a safety risk for agents that keep learning after deployment.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single arXiv preprint. The Trust-Memevo benchmark was built by the same authors who propose the TAME fix, so the problem and the solution are evaluated on authors' own terms. The headline accuracy gain is reported on AIME, a math benchmark, not on an agentic safety setting. No independent replication is visible.
findings.supporting_excerpt: we construct the Trust-Memevo benchmark and find that agents exhibit an overall decline in trustworthiness across multiple tasks during benign task evolution

findings.claim: Tool-using agents have a wider attack surface than chat models, because compromised tool outputs and injected instructions are threat channels in addition to adversarial user prompts. One preprint claims that frontier models lower attack barriers enough to make current alignment frameworks inadequate for deployment.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: All three sources are arXiv preprints and are not peer reviewed. The 'inadequate for real-world deployment' statement is the authors' framing to motivate their own method. It is not an empirical finding in the abstract. The threat models come from papers that propose defences, so severity may be emphasised.
findings.supporting_excerpt: advanced frontier AI models drastically lower attack barriers, rendering current agent alignment frameworks inadequate for real-world deployment.

findings.claim: Whether agent safety can be improved without losing task performance is contested. One paper says existing methods often trade away utility, while others claim their own methods avoid the trade-off. The claims rest on author-selected benchmarks and relative gains, which makes the contradiction hard to resolve.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: FATE's abstract states the trade-off as a problem with existing methods. The other three preprints each claim to solve or reduce it. Some use self-built benchmarks, and results are given as relative reductions in attack success rate (e.g. '3x', '33.5%') without baseline absolute rates in the visible abstracts. Small models (0.8B-8B) are used in some. All are preprints, so it is unclear whether the gains hold against adaptive attackers or in real deployments.
findings.supporting_excerpt: improving agent safety comes at the cost of degraded task performance

findings.claim: The reliability-prediction result looks strong but is weakened by how it was built. Success labels were reconstructed from aggregate score distributions rather than observed per instance, so the very high ROC-AUC (0.970) may reflect the label construction and not real predictive power.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The abstract itself says the target is a modeling assumption. Features such as task difficulty and no-progress behaviour may partly encode the aggregate scores used to build the labels. That leakage risk is my inference, not something the paper states. The data is one benchmark of 696 trajectories across 116 tasks.
findings.supporting_excerpt: the binary target is reconstructed from official model-by-category score distributions and treated as a modeling assumption.

findings.claim: Evidence on the robustness of multi-agent LLM coordination is thin in this set. The only directly relevant paper is a 2024 preprint whose resilience claims are theoretical, backed by empirical validation and a sensor-network case study. LLM agent hallucination and adversarial agents are treated as motivation, not measured.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: This is a single arXiv preprint (not peer reviewed) and about two years old. The abstract does not report tests with real LLM agents at scale. Absence of such evidence here is a gap, not proof of failure.

findings.claim: Standardised, validated methods for reporting agent reliability are still immature. A proposed assurance framework (ARAF) with a six-metric profile is conceptual and explicitly unvalidated, so there is no agreed way to show when an agent is ready for greater autonomy.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: ARAF is a narrative review hosted on Zenodo, a repository that does not peer review. It says it specifies a validation plan, not results. The other two sources each define their own taxonomy and benchmark, which suggests fragmentation across competing evaluation schemes. That reading is my inference.
findings.supporting_excerpt: No new experimental results are claimed.

hype_flags: 'Safety and effectiveness can be jointly optimized' - based on self-built and selected benchmarks in preprints, with a contradicting statement from another paper about existing trade-offs
'Comparable to leading closed-source models' with ~1k training samples (AgentDoG 1.5) - an authors' claim on their own benchmarks, not independently verified
Test-time memory evolution framed as 'pivotal for AGI' - the same paper finds trustworthiness declines during benign evolution
ROC-AUC of 0.970 for success prediction - labels were reconstructed from aggregate scores, not observed
Benchmark 'task success' as a readiness signal - about 31% of successes in one benchmark still failed harness criteria
'Provable resilience' for multi-agent LLM systems - supported only by a 2024 preprint with a sensor-network case study

finding.claim: S2 describes the result as 'process-level behavioral drift', but the study did not observe drift over time. It compared 240 trials across skills, spec variants, harnesses and models in one enterprise system. The abstract says longitudinal validation under actual API evolution is future work. The 92.6% figure counts deviations flagged by the authors' own template checks (tool selection, arguments, order, database integrity), not demonstrated harm. It also comes from a single preprint and one proprietary use case, so the generalisation to 'enterprise agents' is overstated.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract reports 162 of 175 final-check-passing trials with an 'evaluator-detected deviation' and applies the framework to one Value Aware Resiliency system. It frames longitudinal validation as remaining future work. A deviation from a prescribed trajectory is not necessarily an error. The abstract does not say how many deviations changed outcomes.

finding.claim: S6 presents the 'structural' failure of binary detectors and the perfect agent F1 as a general finding. The paper's own results are limited to a controlled benchmark of browser-automation agents, with 100% recall resting on two features. The authors say the signal is a Playwright artifact. A detector built on it may fail for agents that use real input devices, human-in-the-loop operation, API-only access or other automation stacks. A perfect F1 across 30 runs on a self-built benchmark also suggests an easy, possibly saturated test.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The authors themselves tie detection to a tooling artifact. That limits how far 'perfect F1' can be read as evidence for agent detection in general. It is a single preprint with a self-constructed benchmark.
finding.supporting_excerpt: The discriminative signal is a browser-automation artifact, not evidence of agent reasoning: Playwright does not emit the raw pointer-move and wheel-delta streams a physical input device produces
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S3 is labelled verified_fact, but the claim that these vulnerabilities are not addressed by frameworks or by agent research is the authors' own assertion from their experience with typical agent workflows. It is not an independently verified fact. The paper is a mid-2024 preprint and may be dated, since agent frameworks and safety work have moved quickly. The finding also omits that the paper proposes defences evaluated only by its own experiments.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract bases the claim on the authors' experience and on defences they designed and tested themselves. The 'not addressed by' statement is a self-reported gap, not a survey result. Later alignment papers in the evidence set (e.g. src_302c5699ae) address tool-channel threats, which weakens the 'not addressed' framing.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Through studying and experiencing the workflow of typical AI agents, we have raised several concerns regarding their security.

finding.claim: S4 says 'multiple works' converge on a framing that extends established protocols rather than replacing them. The two sources differ in kind. src_1b70ec88bc extends OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, so it is compatible with existing protocols. src_ca33c17412 calls itself a preliminary, falsifiable hypothesis with a zk-SNARK proof of concept. It argues that existing mechanisms lack cryptographic evidence of policy satisfaction. Presenting a hypothesis and a framework proposal as a converging research direction overstates maturity, and 'rather than replacing' fits only one of the two.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstracts describe proposals, not validated or deployed systems. Neither reports adoption or security evaluation against real attacks. The two works also take different positions on compatibility with existing identity and access infrastructure.
finding.supporting_excerpt: This study hypothesizes that agent authorization can be formalized as a cryptographically verifiable relation

finding.claim: S11 infers a 'shared research direction' from one prototype and one purely theoretical paper. The lakehouse paper is a proof of concept on a single platform (Bauplan) for data-pipeline repair. The actuarial paper establishes mathematical results and defers empirical work to companion papers. Neither shows that runtime gating or proof-carrying checks constrain side effects in realistic, adversarial agent deployments, so the finding overstates the evidential basis.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: One source is a case-study prototype and the other is a foundational theory paper whose empirical companion is separate. A thematic similarity between them is not evidence that the approaches work or are converging.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We present a proof-of-concept in which agents repair data pipelines using correctness checks inspired by proof-carrying code.

finding.claim: Several findings (S5, S9, S12) rest on position, conceptual or governance papers that propose mechanisms but report no empirical test of effectiveness. S5's visibility measures and S9's agent infrastructure are described as 'proposed' or 'an incomplete catalog of research directions'. The findings do not make clear that feasibility, circumvention, and privacy or concentration-of-power costs remain unquantified. The risk is that readers take proposed governance tools to be mature.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstracts describe 'potential implementations' and 'research directions' and give no empirical effectiveness data. The S5 authors themselves flag unresolved negative impacts. The S9 abstract calls its own catalog 'incomplete'.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Further work into understanding the measures and mitigating their negative impacts can help to build a foundation for the governance of AI agents.

limitations: Only abstracts or metadata were available. No method details, effect sizes, confidence intervals or full experimental setups were checked.
Most of the 12 papers are arXiv preprints or Zenodo/small-venue items that have not been through rigorous peer review, and most safety papers propose and evaluate their own methods.
Two papers (src_7ec1f79f00, src_94f0274d75) have no usable abstract, and src_94f0274d75 only repeats its title. They were not used for any finding.
Several abstracts are truncated (src_7bc9fb98fb, src_d30f187234, src_d302498671, src_109719a0f6, src_2bfdb9a6ea), so some conclusions and caveats may be missing.
Coverage is narrow. The set focuses on reliability and safety benchmarks and has little on costs, latency, compute, enterprise adoption, legal liability or competing non-agentic approaches.
The citation count of 24 for src_2bfdb9a6ea, which was published recently in a small journal, is unusually high. I could not verify it, and it was not used as evidence.
The set has no company-level or deployment-level evidence, so no supplier or vendor concentration risk could be assessed.
Only titles and abstracts were available, so I could not check methods, baselines or results sections. Some abstracts are truncated.
Several sources (src_3f9ff28552, src_7ec1f79f00, src_94f0274d75) have no usable abstract, so I could not use them to test any finding.
I did not challenge S1, S7, S8 or the labelling of S10. Their abstracts support the claims as worded, and S7 and S8 are explicitly framed as review or vision positions.
Many of the evidence papers are 2026 preprints with few or no citations, so I could not weigh them against community consensus.

draft.summary: The evidence shows AI agents moving from research to commercial products fast: research mentions of the exact phrase grew from 1,077 works in 2024 to 4,480 in 2025 (+316%), and the current partial year is running at +345% versus the same period, so momentum is still building rather than fading. In parallel, nearly every large enterprise software vendor and several mid-caps now describe shipping agent platforms or features (Salesforce Agentforce, Amazon Bedrock Managed Agents, Microsoft Dynamics, Alphabet Gemini Enterprise, Meta Muse, Oracle OCI, Snowflake's $128.3m Natoma acquisition, plus smaller names such as Atlassian, BILL, Figma, Klaviyo, Amplitude and DigitalOcean). What the evidence does not show is verified end-customer adoption, agent-attributable revenue or pricing power: company filings describe their own products, and the only adoption-like numbers are social posts, which are unverified. The research side simultaneously documents unresolved problems - benchmark design that misleads (S1), process-level deviations hidden by final-output checks (S2, weakened by C1), an unaddressed agent attack surface (S3, weakened by C3), and reliability reporting that is explicitly unvalidated (R8) - while governance and authorization proposals (S4, S5, S9, S11) are conceptual or prototype-stage and challenged (C4, C5, C6). The main uncertainty is therefore not whether agents are being built and sold, but whether reliability, security and accountability mature faster than deployments, and whether any of this converts into durable economics rather than feature parity. Related equities do not give a clean read: four of five agent-linked names checked have pulled back sharply over the past month with elevated volatility (T3-T11). Patent evidence is absent because the patent agent did not run.
draft.plain_summary: AI agents are software programs that can carry out tasks on their own, using tools and other programs, rather than just answering questions. The evidence says this is really taking off: research on it is growing extremely fast, and most big software companies - plus a number of smaller ones - now sell agent products, although none of the company documents show how many customers are actually paying for them. The thing most likely to slow it down is trust: studies in this evidence set show agents can fail quietly, be attacked through the tools they use, and get less reliable as they learn, and there is still no agreed way to prove an agent is safe enough to run without supervision.

Price/timing findings show most related names have pulled back sharply over the past month with elevated volatility (T3, T4, T5, T6, T7, T8, T9, T10, T11), which is risk context only, not a timing signal.

horizons.assessment: The medium-term case rests on agents becoming a standard layer of enterprise software rather than a feature. The evidence for direction is broad but self-reported: nine separate filers describe agent products (M1-M7, M8), and one company explicitly flags that third-party autonomous agents may circumvent its pricing and reduce control over distribution (M9). The evidence does not establish which layer captures the economics - platform, application, data or runtime - and the reliability findings (R1, R2, R8) suggest enterprise deployment depth will depend on tooling that is still immature. No cited finding quantifies market size, win rates or retention.

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: The long-horizon evidence is the overall research trend plus governance proposals, not commercial results: work on agents continues to accelerate (2024: 1,077 works; 2025: 4,480; 2026 partial year 13,252 versus 2,977 at the same point last year), and governance researchers propose identifiers, monitoring and logging as the shape of future regimes (S5) though these are untested (C6). Nothing in the findings supports a specific long-run revenue, margin or market-share path, and the risk work (R1-R8) shows the failure modes that could cap autonomy levels. Long-term confidence is therefore low.

bull.label: ai_interpretation
bull.narrative: Every major enterprise software vendor plus a long tail of mid-caps now ships agent capability, and one paid $128.3m for an agent-connectivity platform, which is evidence of real budgets behind the theme rather than marketing alone (M1-M8, M3). Smaller filers with named agent products and disclosed revenue growth - Atlassian (+26.0%), Klaviyo (+31.6%), Figma (+41.0%), DigitalOcean (+15.5%) - show the theme reaching beyond the mega-caps (K1-K6). Research supply is growing faster than almost any other topic in this evidence set, which supports a deep talent and component pipeline, and governance work is at least converging on concrete mechanisms such as agent identifiers and activity logging (S5, S7).

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: Agents become a normal, widely shipped software layer over 1-5 years, but the commercial evidence so far is company self-description rather than adoption proof, and the reliability and security literature shows the barriers to unattended operation are real. Deployments likely proceed with human oversight first, which delays the operational savings that justify premium pricing; meanwhile competitive intensity is high because nearly every filer in this set offers something similar (M1-M8), and at least one platform company warns agents could erode its own pricing control (M9). The most defensible assumption is breadth of participation with unresolved economics.

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: A material share of the agent case rests on findings the risk layer has already undercut. Process-level reliability numbers come from one preprint and one proprietary use case (C1 attacking S2), the claim that frameworks do not address agent vulnerabilities is the authors' own assertion from a 2024 preprint (C3 against S3), and authorization, proof-carrying and runtime-gating proposals are one prototype and one theoretical paper (C5 against S11). If agents fail visibly - injected tool output, cascading state errors, memory that degrades with self-evolution (R1, R3, R4) - enterprises can slow rollouts, and there is no validated way to prove an agent is ready for more autonomy (R8). Filings already list autonomous agent behaviour as a hard-to-audit risk and agents as a new attack and fraud surface (M10), and Figma states third-party agents may circumvent its pricing (M9). In that world the theme is a cost centre and a liability line rather than a revenue driver.

themes.name: Reliability, security and evaluation tooling for agents
technologies: agent failure taxonomies and benchmarking harnesses
runtime action gating and proof-carrying correctness checks

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: The gap is documented but the tooling evidence is early. Detailed failure taxonomies show frequent recoverable errors (tool use, state tracking) alongside rarer highly critical ones (validation, output) that can cascade (R1), and process-level checks catch deviations that final-output tests miss (S2, though C1 limits that result). One benchmark finds about 31% of successful runs still fail a reliability criterion (R2). Set against that, the assurance framework proposed for reporting agent reliability is explicitly conceptual and unvalidated (R8), and the strongest-looking prediction result may be inflated by how its labels were built (R6). No cited finding names a vendor selling or a customer paying for this tooling, so near-term evidence is problem definition, not market.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: If enterprises expand agent autonomy, standardised evaluation and guardrails become a prerequisite, and the research direction is real: alignment work, failure-trajectory self-evolution, and harness reliability benchmarking all exist (R2, R4, R5). But the evidence for a durable commercial layer is absent here - it rests on the implication of vendor risk disclosures (M10) rather than on any tooling company, contract or deployment named in these findings. Whether safety can be improved without losing utility is openly contested (R5), which is exactly the question a buyer would need answered.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Over 3-5 years the plausible shape is agent identity, monitoring and logging embedded in governance regimes, as proposed by visibility and infrastructure papers (S5, S9), and cryptographically or formally verifiable authorization binding agent, request, context and policy (S4). The findings give no basis to size that market or to say who supplies it: the authorization direction is one framework proposal plus one explicit hypothesis-with-PoC (C4), the runtime gating direction is one prototype and one theoretical paper (C5), and the governance mechanisms are untested proposals with unquantified circumvention and privacy costs (C6). Long-horizon confidence is low.

bull.label: ai_interpretation
bull.narrative: The failure evidence is unusually concrete for a young field, which is what a tooling market needs to form: documented failure taxonomies with severity and cascading behaviour (R1), benchmarks showing final success masks unreliable runs (R2), and a clear statement that no agreed, validated way to report agent reliability exists (R8). Multi-agent coordination robustness and memory-driven trust decay are flagged as open problems with early methods attached (R3, R7), and agent-specific attack channels via tools and injected instructions are identified rather than hypothetical (R4). Governance research converges on concrete mechanisms - agent identifiers, real-time monitoring, activity logging (S5) - and on authorization bound to request, context and policy (S4), which is the earliest plausible form of an enforceable control plane.

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: Evaluation, alignment and governance remain primarily research and framework activity in this evidence set, with adoption pulled along by platform vendors embedding their own guardrails rather than by a distinct tooling market. Progress is real but incremental: methods exist, results are contested, and the strongest quantitative claims are the ones most vulnerable to methodological criticism (R5, R6, R7, C1, C4, C5). Expect capability and constraint to advance together, with supervision levels rising slowly because no validated readiness test exists (R8).

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: The bear case is that the constraint layer stays academic and gets absorbed into platform features at no separate margin. The evidence supports this reading: no company in these findings is named as selling reliability, evaluation or governance tooling, the assurance framework is explicitly unvalidated (R8), the most impressive predictive result may reflect label construction rather than predictive power (R6), multi-agent robustness evidence is a 2024 preprint with theoretical resilience claims (R7), and several headline 'solutions' are one prototype or one hypothesis (C4, C5). Where safety methods do work, the literature disputes whether they cost task performance (R5), which removes the buyer's main reason to pay separately. Meanwhile governance mechanisms such as visibility and logging are proposals with unquantified feasibility, circumvention and privacy costs (C6), and proposed agent authorization standards could equally be delivered by incumbent identity vendors.

themes.name: Agent authorization, identity and agent-to-agent commerce rails

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: The only near-term evidence of agent-to-agent and agent-to-commerce infrastructure comes from social posts, which are unverified claims and cannot carry a rating: reportedly a Personal Agent Protocol 0.1 with OAuth-style scoped auth from payment and commerce providers, and a crypto-cloud service letting agents buy API calls (X2). On the filing side, the concrete evidence is a company paying $128.3m for an enterprise Model Context Protocol platform (M3) and a design platform opening its MCP server to third-party agents in March 2026 while warning those agents may circumvent its pricing (M9). The research side offers one protocol extension and one self-described preliminary hypothesis with a zk-SNARK proof of concept (S4, C4). Near-term evidence is therefore thin and mostly directional.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: The medium-term question is whether agent authorization settles into extensions of existing identity and access protocols or into a new layer. The evidence points at extension in one case (an OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect extension) and at a replacement-style argument in another that existing mechanisms lack cryptographic evidence of policy satisfaction (S4, C4), so the outcome is genuinely open. Governance proposals for agent identifiers, real-time monitoring and activity logging (S5) would, if adopted, create the identifiers such commerce would need, but they report no empirical test (C6). No finding names a customer, standard body adoption or contract for this layer.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Over 3-5 years the plausible long-horizon story - agents transacting, delegating and being held accountable through verifiable authorization and external infrastructure - is exactly the part of the evidence base that is least tested. The infrastructure argument that internal shaping is insufficient and shared protocols for attributing and remedying actions are needed is an unverified claim in this set (S9), runtime gating and proof-carrying checks are one prototype and one theoretical paper (S11, C5), and the actuarial per-action gating idea defers empirical work to companion papers (C5). Confidence is low and the shape, if any, cannot be inferred from these findings.

bull.label: ai_interpretation
bull.narrative: If agents are to act autonomously on behalf of users and firms, they need identity, scoped permissions and an auditable record, and the research direction is moving toward binding the agent, its request, the execution context and policy satisfaction into a verifiable relation that extends established protocols rather than replacing them (S4). Governance work already proposes the ingredients - agent identifiers, real-time monitoring, activity logging applicable from centralized to decentralized deployments (S5) - and external agent infrastructure is argued as a necessary complement to internal shaping (S9). On the commercial side, platforms are already standardising agent-to-tool connectivity: a $128.3m acquisition of an enterprise MCP platform (M3) and a design platform opening its MCP server to third-party agents (M9), with reported commerce and crypto-rail experiments in the social data (X2).

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: Authorization and agent commerce most likely arrive as extensions to identity and access systems that enterprises already run, with agent identifiers and scoped credentials added by existing suppliers, rather than as a new verifiable-authorization layer. The filing evidence supports connectivity standardisation (M3, M9) more than it supports new authorization primitives, and the strongest research claims are a hypothesis with a proof of concept and a prototype (C4, C5). Access to agent-mediated commerce could also cut both ways for platform owners, as one filing warns agents may circumvent pricing and reduce control over distribution and monetization (M9).

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: The bear case is that this is a standards problem with no clear revenue pool and a governance problem with no enforcement. The infrastructure argument is an unverified claim in this evidence set (S9), visibility mechanisms are proposals with unquantified feasibility, circumvention and privacy or concentration-of-power costs (C6), and the two most concrete control-plane works are one prototype and one theoretical paper (C5, S11) plus one protocol extension and one falsifiable hypothesis (C4). Meanwhile the only near-term commerce signals are unverified social posts (X2), and the clearest commercial fact in the theme - a platform opening its MCP server - came with an explicit warning that third-party agents may undermine its pricing and control over distribution (M9). If that dynamic spreads, agent connectivity could be value-destructive for incumbent application layers rather than accretive.

dimension_ratings.rationale: Code-computed OpenAlex counts for the exact phrase 'AI agents' rose from 1,077 works in 2024 to 4,480 in 2025 (+316% YoY), and the current partial year is running at 13,252 versus 2,977 at the same point in 2025 (+345%), indicating momentum is still building rather than fading.
