dimension_ratings.label: assumption
dimension_ratings.note: no supporting finding cited, so treated as an assumption
dimension_ratings.rationale: No patent evidence exists in this version: the patent agent did not run and there are no patent findings and no code-computed patent counts. The only patent-adjacent data point is a company-scout note that Capgemini has 0 patents and 1 paper on the topic, which is not a market-level momentum measure. Rating this dimension would require inventing evidence.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Agents demonstrably run and are shipping in products (M1-M8), so this is beyond pure theory. But the findings show unresolved core problems: final-output tests miss process-level deviations in tool selection, arguments, execution order and database integrity (S2, with C1 limiting the strength of that specific result), about 31% of successful runs still fail a reliability criterion in one benchmark (R2), highly critical validation and output failures can cascade (R1), tool use widens the attack surface via compromised outputs and injected instructions (R4), and memory-driven self-evolution can reduce trustworthiness (R3). Whether safety can be improved without losing utility is contested (R5). Capability is proven; dependable autonomy is not.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Commercial readiness is well evidenced at the product level: Salesforce markets Agentforce across business functions (M1), Amazon offers a public preview of Bedrock Managed Agents and Strands Box (M2), Snowflake paid $128.3m for Natoma, an enterprise MCP platform (M3), Microsoft ships agentic AI in Dynamics (M4), Alphabet offers Gemini Enterprise (M5), Meta launched Muse (M6), Oracle embeds agentic AI in OCI (M7), and six mid- and small-cap software companies commercialised or launched agent products in 2025-2026 (M8, K1-K6). Rated 4 rather than 5 because the evidence is vendor self-description of products, with no cited disclosure of agent-attributable revenue, pricing or unit economics.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: There is no verified customer-adoption evidence in this set. Market findings describe companies' own products and risk disclosures, which does not establish that customers are buying or deploying them; the only adoption-like number - a claim that over half of enterprises already run agentic AI in production - is an unverified social post (X4). The strongest indirect signals are that vendors keep investing (M3 acquisition, M8 launches) and that filers treat agents as a competitive and security risk, which implies awareness rather than proven purchase (M9, M10). Rated 2 on the strength of those indirect signals only.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Industry commitment is broad and specific: a $128.3m acquisition of an enterprise agent-connectivity platform (M3), new managed agent services (M2), agent capability embedded across Microsoft (M4), Alphabet (M5), Meta (M6) and Oracle (M7) portfolios, Agentforce marketed as a platform by Salesforce (M1), agent products launched by six mid- and small-caps (M8, K1-K6), and Meta explicitly saying it expects to increase agentic AI investment while acknowledging it may not generate profits from it (M6). The scale of committed spend is clear even though the returns are not.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: The field is crowded at every layer, which limits any single player's defensibility: four mega-cap platforms (M4, M5, M6, M7) plus Salesforce (M1), Amazon (M2) and Oracle (M7) all ship agents, and at least six smaller software companies have their own agent offerings (M8, K1-K6), so differentiation is unclear from these findings. Two findings suggest position can be actively eroded by agents: one platform warns third-party autonomous agents may circumvent its pricing and reduce its control over distribution and monetization (M9), and competitive disruption from autonomous agents is a cited risk theme (M10). Aggregate-hosted data and workflow incumbency is a plausible advantage, but no finding quantifies share, retention or switching costs.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Evidence on the agent supply chain is indirect: a managed service for building and deploying production agents with an open-source sandbox for behaviour rules (M2) and the acquisition and embedding of an enterprise Model Context Protocol platform for agent connectivity (M3) imply that a tooling and protocol layer exists. Beyond that, the findings say nothing about capacity, pricing, critical dependencies, model access or the reliability of underlying providers, and the claim that frameworks like LangChain, LangGraph and MCP are becoming mainstream developer skills is an unverified social signal (X6). Rated 2 on connectivity evidence alone.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Level 3 (elevated): agents are demonstrably in production or public preview with real customers implied by paid products and a large acquisition (M1, M2, M3, M8), which rules out levels 4-5, but scaling, cost and dependable autonomy remain unproven and several open issues are documented. Reliability failures can cascade and final success masks them (R1, R2), tool-based attacks widen the surface (R4), memory-based self-evolution can reduce trustworthiness (R3), and there is no agreed, validated way to show an agent is ready for greater autonomy (R8). Governance and authorization proposals are untested and challenged (C4, C5, C6), several science findings are weakened by risk challenges (C1, C2, C3), and one filer states agents may undermine its pricing (M9) while several cite agents as an attack and fraud vector (M10). Timing context adds risk but does not decide the level: most agent-linked names have pulled back sharply over the past month with high volatility, and Microsoft sits near its recent average near a 100-day high with little cushion (T1-T11).

missing_data: Patent evidence: the patent agent did not run, so there is no patent count, no assignee data and no basis for a patent_momentum rating - Excel-like patent activity may look very different from the research and product picture.
Verified customer adoption: no finding gives agent customer counts, deployment volumes, win rates, retention or renewal data. The only adoption-like figure is an unverified social post (X4).

Agent-attributable economics: no finding discloses agent-specific revenue, pricing, gross margin, attach rate or cost-to-serve for any vendor, so the commercial importance of agents relative to existing products cannot be assessed.

Validation of governance and reliability mechanisms: proposed visibility, logging, authorization and runtime-gating mechanisms are untested, with circumvention, privacy and cost consequences unquantified (C4, C5, C6).

Longitudinal reliability data: the process-level evaluation study is cross-sectional in a single enterprise system, and its authors list longitudinal validation under real API evolution as future work (C1).
No company evidence yet for a standalone reliability, evaluation or governance tooling vendor: no cited finding names a company selling or a customer buying such tooling.

Market-side agent-commerce and payment-rail projects appear only as social posts and are unverified (X2), and the claim that MCP, LangChain and LangGraph are mainstream developer skills is likewise social-only (X6).
Third-party market data: no firm-level revenue estimates, market-size forecasts, TAM and deal-value benchmarks appear in the findings.
Macro and infrastructure constraints on agent deployment - model cost, latency, compute supply and energy - are not addressed by any finding in this set.
limitations: This assessment is built only from the findings supplied. Several topics that matter for an investment view (patents, verified adoption, pricing, margins, market size) have no evidence here, and those gaps are recorded in missing_data rather than filled.

The research-activity metric counts only works whose title or abstract contains the exact phrase 'AI agents'. Synonyms and abbreviations are excluded and the count is not normalised for overall growth in publishing, so the growth rate overstates the topic's relative share of science. The current year is partial.

A large part of the scientific evidence is preprints and abstract-level analysis with medium or low source confidence, and the risk challenges (C1-C6) show that several prominent findings overstate their basis, come from a single study, or are position papers rather than tested work.

Market findings are company self-description in SEC filings plus news headlines that were not read; a company describing a technology is not proof of customer adoption, and headlines are unverified claims given little weight.

X findings are social posts from approved accounts in the last 7 days. They indicate what companies are announcing or emphasising, not what is true, and several of the most commercially suggestive items (agent commerce rails, enterprise adoption rates) exist only there.
Patent evidence is entirely absent because the patent agent did not run, so no statement about intellectual-property position, freedom to operate or patent-based momentum is possible.

Price and timing findings cover a short ~100-trading-day window for a subset of companies and are used strictly as risk context; they cannot speak to valuation, entry points or expected returns, and this assessment deliberately contains no price targets or recommendations of any kind.

Horizon views mix verified facts with interpretation and forecast labels, but the underlying evidence is heavily weighted to the last 12-18 months, so statements about 3-5 years are inherently speculative and marked with low confidence where they are made at all.
